headline: High: caveman’s MCP-enabled content-writing workflow can ingest and act on shared files, creating medium prompt-injection and data-leakage risks with awesome-python’s file-centric, non-networked profile.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: caveman explicitly uses MCP and reads/writes files like CLAUDE.md, so it can ingest attacker-controlled content; awesome-python is a file-based collection with no isolation or provenance controls. The pair lacks a documented shared channel, but the file bridge is enough to make instruction hijacking plausible.
conditions: IF caveman reads content from a shared workspace or CLAUDE.md that awesome-python can influence, injection is possible.
IF the orchestrator copies awesome-python content into caveman’s prompt context, caveman may follow embedded instructions.
mitigations: Separate workspaces for the two agents.
Strip or quote untrusted file content before caveman reads it.
Disable MCP access for untrusted repositories.
Add a provenance banner to all imported text.
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization at the orchestrator boundary.

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-python has no data classes touched and no network egress, while caveman touches session logs, memory files, and project notes. There is no evidence of shared secrets or outbound exfiltration, so leakage is limited to local workspace spillover rather than third-party disclosure.
conditions: IF both agents share the same filesystem, caveman may read files created by awesome-python.
IF sensitive notes are stored in caveman’s memory files, they can be exposed to the other agent’s workspace.
mitigations: Use separate directories per agent.
Keep sensitive notes out of shared folders.
Run caveman with a minimal workspace mount.
Rotate or delete transient memory files after each run.
requires-engineering: add per-agent access controls.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: awesome-python is non-runnable and has no write or network surfaces, so it cannot contend for mutable resources. caveman supports multiple instances, but the profile does not show overlapping write targets or shared locks, making direct capability conflict unlikely.
conditions: IF caveman instances are pointed at the same writable directory, file clobbering becomes possible.
IF an external orchestrator maps both agents onto one mutable workspace, conflicts can occur.
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories.
Serialize writes through one coordinator.
Avoid concurrent edits to the same files.
Check for stale lockfiles before starting.
requires-engineering: implement workspace locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: caveman is a content-writing agent that can consume files and produce downstream text, while awesome-python is a curated collection that may be treated as authoritative source material. If the orchestrator feeds awesome-python-derived content into caveman without verification, errors can cascade into generated outputs.
conditions: IF awesome-python content is imported into caveman prompts without review, caveman may propagate mistakes.
IF caveman is tasked to draft user-facing text from repository content, unverified claims can be amplified.
mitigations: Require human review of imported facts.
Mark repository text as untrusted input.
Add a verification step before drafting.
Limit caveman to summarization, not assertion.
requires-engineering: add citation checking in the pipeline.

E_compliance.rationale: No residency, certification, retention, or regulated data classes are documented for either agent. awesome-python touches no data classes, and caveman’s listed data classes are operational metadata rather than regulated content, so no compliance mismatch is evidenced.
conditions: IF regulated data such as PHI or EU PII is introduced into caveman’s memory files, compliance review is required.
IF a deployment adds residency or retention constraints not shown here, the assessment changes.
mitigations: Do not store regulated data in shared notes.
Review retention settings before deployment.
Keep operational logs separate from user content.
